title: Card skimming and digital pickpocketing
body_md:
## Two kinds of card-data theft
A physical skimmer is an added or hidden reader in an ATM or point-of-sale terminal; a camera or keypad overlay may capture the PIN. Some devices are deep inside the reader, so a normal appearance is **not proof of safety**. The US Secret Service advises preferring supervised ATMs, looking for tampering, covering PIN entry and enabling transaction alerts. Inspect gently; do not dismantle or handle a suspected device. Tell staff and choose another terminal.

Digital e-skimming is different: unauthorized code on a payment page can copy entered card data while a genuine purchase still succeeds. PCI SSC addresses this chiefly through merchant controls over payment-page scripts; a consumer cannot reliably spot malicious JavaScript by eye. HTTPS protects data in transit but cannot prove a merchant or its page is uncompromised. Browser extensions with broad page access add another exposure; grant only necessary permissions and remove unused extensions. Open Wi-Fi alone is not a reliable explanation for modern HTTPS checkout theft.

When available, a supported contactless wallet can substitute a payment token for the card number; an issuer virtual card may limit where a credential works. Features vary, and neither makes a dishonest merchant safe. Also set issuer alerts and review statements. If a charge is unfamiliar, check whether it is a merchant descriptor, pending authorization or family purchase without delaying a call to the issuer when fraud is plausible. Use the issuer's app or the number on your card, freeze/replace as advised and dispute accurately. For a Russian unauthorized card debit, the Bank of Russia says to promptly notify/block through the bank, get a statement, contest the operation and report theft; local rules elsewhere differ.

widget_config.goal: Reduce card-data exposure at terminals and online checkouts, then respond correctly to a suspicious charge.
widget_config.today_action: Turn on issuer transaction alerts and find the card-freeze control in your bank app before you need it.
widget_config.scope: Physical advice: US Secret Service February 2025; digital threat: PCI SSC March 2025; tokenization: Visa; Russian response: Bank of Russia. Features and rights vary, checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: US Secret Service: ATM & POS Terminal Skimming (February 2025)
sources.scope: US advisory on physical skimmers, PIN shielding, alerts and reporting; February 2025.

sources.title: PCI SSC: Payment Page Security and Preventing E-Skimming
sources.scope: March 2025 merchant/service-provider guidance on browser payment-page scripts; not a consumer detector.

sources.title: Visa: What is Tokenisation?
sources.scope: Visa explanation of replacing card number with payment token; implementation varies by wallet/provider.

sources.title: Google Chrome Help: Install and Manage Extensions
sources.scope: Chrome-specific controls for extension access to website data; not a skimmer detector.

sources.title: Bank of Russia: Unauthorized Card Debits
sources.scope: Russian cardholder steps for an unauthorized debit; not an automatic refund rule.

blocks.title: A loose reader at a station ATM
blocks.situation: Synthetic: the card slot on an unsupervised station ATM looks raised and the keypad surround moves. You have not inserted a card.
blocks.analysis: The anomaly warrants choosing a different machine and telling the operator; it is not your job to prove a crime by pulling parts off. If you already used it, contact your issuer for card and PIN advice and watch alerts.

blocks.title: A restaurant preauthorization
blocks.situation: Synthetic: after paying by phone wallet, your app shows the restaurant’s name and a pending amount slightly above the bill. Staff explain a preauthorization and provide a receipt.
blocks.analysis: A pending amount can be legitimate, but do not assume it will settle correctly. Keep the receipt, check the final posting and ask the issuer if it remains wrong. Wallet use reduces card-number exposure but does not settle billing disputes automatically.

blocks.title: The travel payment trail
blocks.setup: Synthetic: you need cash at a station and later pay online. Decide across physical and digital exposure; no real card data is used.

steps.prompt: The station ATM reader is loose. What do you do?

choices.text: Insert the card to see if it works.
choices.consequence: The test may expose card data.
choices.explanation: Do not test suspected skimmers with your card.

choices.text: Leave it, notify the operator and use a supervised alternative.
choices.consequence: You avoid a visible anomaly without touching evidence.
choices.explanation: A visible problem justifies changing machines.

steps.prompt: The next ATM looks normal. What additional action helps?

choices.text: Shield the PIN and keep transaction alerts active.
choices.consequence: A camera sees less, and unexpected use can be noticed.
choices.explanation: A hidden reader may be invisible; layers still matter.

choices.text: Assume appearance alone rules out skimming.
choices.consequence: An internal device would go unnoticed.
choices.explanation: Normal appearance is not a safety certificate.

steps.prompt: An online checkout has HTTPS. What does it tell you?

choices.text: No e-skimmer can exist on this page.
choices.consequence: Malicious scripts may run on encrypted pages.
choices.explanation: Encryption does not validate page code.

choices.text: Traffic is encrypted; still verify seller and use suitable payment protection.
choices.consequence: You account for both transport and merchant risk.
choices.explanation: Payment-page code can be compromised despite HTTPS.

steps.prompt: A small unfamiliar charge appears. What is the first safe route?

choices.text: Use the issuer app or card number, check descriptor and report if still unexplained.
choices.consequence: The issuer can assess the charge and card controls.
choices.explanation: Do not give card details to a number in a suspicious alert.

choices.text: Reply with card details to the alert message.
choices.consequence: You may hand sensitive data to an impostor.

blocks.debrief: Physical inspection helps but misses hidden devices; payment tokens and alerts reduce exposure or time to detection. The issuer handles an actual charge.

questions.prompt: A terminal looks clean. Can it still contain a skimmer?

choices.text: Yes; some devices are internal, so use PIN and monitoring layers.
choices.explanation: The Secret Service describes deeply inserted readers.

choices.text: No; every skimmer is a loose overlay.

questions.prompt: A tokenized wallet payment was made at a dishonest store. What remains?

choices.explanation: No payment token can force delivery.

choices.text: The seller can still fail to deliver; use normal dispute channels.
choices.explanation: Tokenization protects a credential, not the merchant promise.

questions.prompt: An unknown debit appears on a Russian card. What does CBR advise first?

choices.text: Promptly contact/block through the bank and contest the operation.
choices.explanation: The Russian guidance starts with the bank and card block.

choices.text: Wait for the merchant to refund automatically.
